comments.title: Why don't they sing?
comments.content:
Good morning JMG, 

I was interested in a comment made recently that Christianity is unique in its application of collective group singing, which surprised me. I've attended many different kinds of Christian service traditions over the years and I've always felt that collective group singing is a core part of the experience. Churches that leave all the music to the worship team, even a quite good worship team, just don't feel the same at all. Since you have seen a wider set of traditions, have you seen any difference of effect between traditions that have group singing vs non-group singing, or no music at all? Is there a magical component to group singing?

I saw that you don't listen to music during your practices, that makes sense to me.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content:
That's one of the things that baffles me about the prevalence of congregational singing in American Christianity. Most other religions, even in America, don't do anything of the kind and still get good results -- I've attended Shinto and Buddhist services, for example, where there's generally no music at all, and Taoist services, where there's instrumental music played by clergy in the equivalent of minor orders, and in each case there's no sense of anything lacking. I've read that in Christian services in many other parts of the world, music is performed by musicians with or without a trained choir, and the congregation simply listens.

Yet I've heard other people talk about the importance of congregational singing in Christian services here. I'm not at all sure what to make of it.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content:
A bit of history
Early Church (1st–4th Century): Christians sang psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. In the early 2nd century, Pliny the Younger reported Christians gathering to sing hymns to Christ.4th Century: St. Ambrose of Milan popularised congregational hymn singing in the Western church to bolster faith.Medieval Period: Singing largely left to professionals or choirs.Reformation (16th Century): Martin Luther and others reintroduced congregational singing as a central, active part of worship in the vernacular, leading to the first Lutheran hymnals in 1524.18th Century: English congregations widely adopted hymn singing

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content: In a religion (Protestantism) that has deliberately stripped almost all powerful ritual and energy work out the service, singing is one of the only ways to energize and energetically align the worshippers. It’s pretty much the only way to “tap in.” They don’t have the Eucharist like Catholics/Orthodox, for example.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content:
I have sung the Akathist hymn with a bunch of old Greek ladies a few times. No sacraments involved in that service and half the singers had hearing aids, but a very definite (and wonderful!) energetic thing going on. Some combination of the long, long hymn (many many verses!) and the gigantic love and devotion the Yia Yias have for the Theotokos... I don't know but maybe She visits them :)

It was so disappointing when we moved, and our new church just plainchants the verses. The effect is not at all the same. But I can't tell whether it's the singing or the pious-old-lady devotion that does it. I just know that if I get cancer or something, I want the Yia Yias notified immediately!

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content:
One thought that occurs to me, more on the cynical side, is that it is a way to keep the congregation locked into the church egregore.

On the other side of that cynical spectrum, the similar thought occurred to me that it was a way for the congregation to feel like they are the bride of Christ together, as sometimes the collective church is thought of as being.

-JPM

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content:
Could this be a result of the movement away from higher more ritualized “high church” practices? In the Catholic tradition group singing is considered part of the “constant prayer” of the church. (Which is why Gregorian chanting is/was so formalized and associated with monastics.)

As the energetic focus shifted from an ritual act by a single officiant, to a gestalt of the whole congregation group singing seems like a good way to build up “group” energy without the focused energy and intent of a ritual leader/cleric.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content: The Latin Novus Ordo Mass in Chicago that I attend over the summer doesn't have congregational singing. Not sure how you can get congregational singing when the pieces sung are random Gregorian Chants in Latin or works by the likes of Palestrina or Bach.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content:
There is this kind of weird brain wave synchronization that happens when people play/create music together. I read about a study that monitored the brain waves of a small improvisational jazz band while they played together and it was like they became a group mind, with synchronized patterns across all members. And when you think about things like how sea shanties were used to coordinate actions of sailors it seems clear to me that one of them magical aspects of music is that it can temporarily create a coordinated whole from many individuals.

Maybe this more participatory music magic comes more from African traditions? Certainly the African American churchs have had an enormous impact with Gospel Music.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content: Well, that's probably why it doesn't work for me; being autistic, I don't pick up on those synchronizing processes at all. It's the same reason I don't enjoy sports games, rock concerts, or tent revivals -- everyone else is caught up in a groupmind and I'm on the outside looking in.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content:
This is huge. Singing (and dancing) as a group is pretty universal, and it seems to serve the function of synchronizing the members of the group-- whether that's for practical purposes (timing the axes so nobody gets injured: the Parchman Farm recordings have some examples of this), social purposes, spiritual purposes... it works on a lot of levels. The very recent habit of exclusively listening to music rather than participating in it is, imo, a civilization-level disaster. And I say that as someone who, like our generous host, doesn't get any of that group-melding benefit from it! I'm still a member of the church choir, because I believe it's that important.

Way more than just African traditions. Experienced some far-out things with east Asians doing group religious chants. I can't say exactly *what* was going on there, but it was definitely something way beyond the people and voices in that room. Suspect this is present in a lot of cultures, in some form or other.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content: There's a similar thing that happens in equestrian activities, if both the horse and the rider are focusing strongly on the same particular tricky technical task (a jumping track with tight spacing requiring complex judgements of step counts and placement, or sometimes "dressage"/precisely-controlled prancing and pacing) and have a lot of practice picking up each others' cues of possibility/doubt and intention/reluctance.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content:
There's a very insightful book on all this: Keeping Together in Time by William H. McNeil (1995).

In addition to group singing, line-dancing, and playing music together, military drill is an excellent example of the phenomenon, as is the crew-work on a ship at sea timed by the songs of the shanty-man. The same phenomenon is produced by the old-fashioned drill work used in some of the fraternal lodges. (One of my great-grandfathers was a member of the Woodsmen of the World, and they had ax-drills at some of their meetings. I don't happen to know whether they drilled with sharpened axes or dull ones, but if with sharpened ones, a missed movement would have had severe consequences. Likewise, a line of men mowing a hay-field with scythes has to move very precisely together in time, or they will get badly wounded.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content: Hmm! I learned fraternal military drill in the uniformed branch of the Odd Fellows, a good many years ago. It's the one activity of this kind that worked fairly well for me. We didn't use sharpened swords, btw, but a little clumsiness could still have caused wounds.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content:
In that case, may I share a data point anecdote from this past weekend?

I sing rather well. I was raised Church of Christ (the no-instruments kind) and so I am used to the entire congregation singing. I became Catholic and have remained so for nearly 20 years, and while Catholics possess a rich musical heritage, in practice very few Catholics do the singing even though they are supposed to. It has happened a few times that I am the only person in the congregation singing - and yes, these are the parts the congregation is supposed to sing. I've also done my time as cantor, in worship teams, and many different choirs.

I have a monthly military drill weekend, and after release I try to get to the closest local parish for their service.

This past weekend I arrived late. The service was half over. When I entered, only the cantor was singing what was clearly intended to be a group effort, but the whole congregation was mute. The effect in the space was like having only a quarter pat of butter for a large slice of bread. I joined in, and after a few surprised looks, in short order many of the congregants started to sing, too. The woman next to me was moved to tears and hugs by the experience. The character of the service immediately and palpably changed, even to my relatively untrained subtle senses.

Afterwards, I had what must've been half the congregation line up to shake my hands. Everyone said they enjoyed the experience and were happy to join in.

That's gratifying to my ego, but I really genuinely wish that everyone would sing just as much as I do. In some places, like an Anglican ordinariate, there would be nothing remarkable about what I'm doing.

What gets me is this: *if they all like singing, why don't they sing (without me)?* They're all there, it's the appointed singing-time. There's a cantor, the words are projected for everyone to see. The songs are not complex or difficult. Is this a generational thing (the entire congregation was boomer-aged), a spiritual thing, or something else? They want to, clearly. It seems to me that if you have a room full of people that want to do something, but they won't, that there might be some kind of psycho-spiritual block there.


I hadn't realized that the other religious musical traditions were clergy or professionals-only. Has that always been the case or is that a 20th century development? I didn't know that shomyo or Tibetan chants were monks-only activities.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content:
1) We live in a society where creative activities are increasingly restricted to professionals for marketing purposes -- don't you dare sing or play an instrument, we've got recordings to sell you! That sort of programming has to be fought consciously, and not everyone thinks of that.

2) I have yet to hear a Buddhist congregation join in the chanting. Maybe it's done in some denominations, but not the ones I've attended.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content: In the Soto Zen services that I have attended, everyone chants. The Zen center my husband belongs to chanted a portion of their Sunday service as part of the St. Louis Interfaith Partnership's "Chanters, Cantors, and Choirs" event last week.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content: Hmm! Learn something new every day...

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content:
I've been at Tibetan Buddhist practices sessions in which everyone chanted (or sang) together, sometimes led off by an appointed chant master. Shingon services can also feature group chanting.

Christian monastics (Orthodox and Catholic) also sing or chant together.

In these situations, the chanting or singing is generally practice rather than performance. Of course, there are situations in which the practice becomes a performance for spectators who are not expected to participate.

People in 20th+ century US are generally hesitant, or resistant, to participate in group singing or chanting perhaps because they are accustomed to thinking of it as a performance by experts. Up through the 29th century this wasn't the case, and people expected, and were expected, to join in group song, chant, and prayer.

Spiritualist seances often enough led off with some hymn-singing, which was often described rather sarcastically by unsympathetic observers. I suppose this was part of the transition from practice to performance -- but I think, from the Spiritualist point of view, the idea of having a specialist choir sing the hymns would have missed the point of them.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content:
Back when I was part of the coven in the Fort Campbell area, we would sing or chant to raise energy. Depending on the moods, the high priest and/or high priestess would sing the calling of the quarters and occasionally even the invitation to the god and goddess we were invoking for that circle. But every circle, we sang or chanted to raise the energy for the group working.

So, it isn't just a Christian thing. Someone else mentioned sea chanties, and I'll add in the military context, calling cadence in formation, whether marching or running.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content:
Christianity is a broad church and in my experience of it, there's little to no congregational singing, but then again, I'm not in the USA. In the Catholic churches I attended in my youth there was only singing at Christmas Mass as that was a special occasion. There was a choir but people were supposed to join in. They stopped doing Midnight Mass on Christmas Eve due to the drunks from the pub going straight to Mass and belting their hearts out.

Nowadays I sometimes attend High Church Anglican services were there is a trained choir of clergy and choristers. The general public don't join in and aren't expected to either. That's for the best really, as I would rather listen to trained singers. There is the Taize phenomenon which is for both Catholics and Protestants but it's not the norm. Anglicans, I notice, do monthly services with Taize singing sometimes.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content: In the Presbyterian churches I attended as a child and teen in the 1960s and early 1970s, there was a choir who sang at least one hymn by itself and other hymns which everyone in the congregation was expected to sing. A pianist or organist played the hymns in four part harmony, so members of the congregation could sing along to whichever part fit their vocal range.

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content: For the record, at the Anglican church I attended as a child in NZ in the 70s, you were handed a hymn book as you entered the church and everyone was expected to sing together (the vicar would indicate the number of each hymn in the book before each hymn so people could find it). I much preferred it when we kids were allowed into the main service rather than being shipped off to the Sunday School in the church hall to do what seemed to me quite inane things like listening to stories from the Bible (I was a reader from an early age so listening to others read was never my thing).

replies.title: Re: Why don't they sing?
replies.content:
Jewish congregations sing—almost all prayer is some form of communal or responsive singing, in every Jewish congregation I have attended of any denomination.

Not all congregations are equally tuneful, though! There was a religious-musical leader named Carlbach who was very influential, and now some congregations even advertise they have “Carlbach kabbalat shabbat”, meaning Friday night prayer meetings welcoming in the Sabbath are long and musical and sometimes improvisational, up to a point. People like it because it increases the kavvanah, the group spiritual intention/intensity.

—Ms. Krieger

replies.title: Re: Weather Prediction
replies.content:
There used to be a great deal of traditional weather-lore, which varied greatly (as it should) from one region to the next. Most of it seems to be long, long forgotten nowadays. Here are four books I find worthwhile on it:

Michael Aislabie Denham. A Collection of Proverbs and Popular Sayings Relating to the Seasons, the Weather, and Agricultural Pursuits. 1846.

H. H. C. Dunwoody. Weather Proverbs. 1883.

Richard Inwards. Weather Lore. 3rd ed. 1898.

Edward B. Garriott. Weather Folk-Lore and Local Weather Signs. 1903.

comments.title: Visuals in Meditation
comments.content:
Hello JMG,
I am a new student of magick, and I have been enjoying my practice of meditation and attention exercises, along with early ritual work. Something interesting has been happening to me and I'm not quite sure what to think of it. Typically I am a highly verbal thinker, and have never really experienced very vivid visual thoughts in my head. During my attention exercises observing verbal thought without attachment has been a major point of focus and improvement. However, in the increasing moments where I am able to find stillness of this verbal thought, I regularly begin seeing things in my head that it feels I have no control over, at least not in a similar way to my verbal thought. At times they feel symbolically significant, but as or more often they feel rather random. On top of that, these things I'm seeing are highly vivid and expansive, which is a rather new experience for me.
On one hand, this is very exciting for me as I feel like a new world of experience is opening up before me that I've never had before. On the other hand it is difficult to not be completely distracted by these visuals, to the point where I almost feel I'm in a trance, forgetting where or who I am for short periods. I'd imagine it is related in some way to beginning to work the visualization muscle (if you will) during ritual work, but I can't say for sure. The reason I'm telling you all of this is in my reading and research, I haven't come across any perspectives talking about this, as it's rather specific. Is this something you've heard of, or is typical of new students? Any perspective or advice on how to approach this generally or during meditation?
Thanks so much for your time!

replies.title: Re: Visuals in Meditation
replies.content: Your mind will throw all sorts of distractions at you during meditation, especially in the early phases. It's essential that you ignore them, and quiet your inner eye as you quiet your inner voice. What you're seeing are astral images; when you get to slightly more advanced practices, you'll be able to develop the capacity to see and work with them -- but your meditation practice has other goals. Stick to those and don't let yourself get distracted.

comments.title: Odin mantra
comments.content:
I'm sorry I missed the discussion with the Vedantist about Odin last week. If that person is reading this week: there's a Heathen chanting practice called "galdr"--traditionally it was a magical incantation in a specific meter, but modern practitioners will chant rune names/sounds to work with their energies...which is a long way of saying there's some precedent for your using mantra to connect with Odin. Of course, as a Hindu practitioner you probably know more than I do about destructive aspects of deity!

--Sister Crow

comments.content: I was raised as a Mason in Nebraska in 2002, I believe. replies.title: Re: Returning to Lodge after 22 years - mostly abroad
replies.content:
Unless you happen to live in one of a very few places, the esoteric side of Masonry tends to be well concealed, and for good reason -- there are actually a lot of Masons who are ordinary, devout Christians and the like, and who bristle at the thought that their beloved Craft has anything esoteric about it. In some jurisdictions, Masons who let on that they're interested in occultism can run into serious trouble, up to and including being thrown out of the Craft for various trumped-up reasons. (I know some guys who are in the middle of a mess like that right now, for example.)

Because of this, what usually happens is that Masons with occult interests tend to choose some specific body as their clubhouse. In one jurisdiction I was active in, it was the York Rite; in certain others, it was the Scottish Rite; in some cities, there's a lodge or two where the occultists belong, and so on. You won't be able to find this out instantly. Become a member of a lodge that seems congenial, watch, listen, and wait for hints -- somebody talking about philosophy, or symbolism, or what have you -- and express interest. They'll sound you out, and encourage you to visit this lodge or apply to that appendant body.
